## Incident Report — MTA 2024-08-15 Traffic Analysis Exercise

**Evidence reviewed:** `2024-08-15-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (18,189 frames). No IDS/Suricata alert export was present in the evidence directory — attribution below is behavioral only.

### Victim host
| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| IPv4 | 10.8.15.133 |
| MAC | 00:1c:bf:03:54:82 (Intel NIC vendor) |
| Hostname | DESKTOP-H8ALZBV |
| Windows domain | lafontainebleu.org (DC at 10.8.15.4, WIN-JEGJIX7Q9RS) |
| Logged-in user | plucero |

Confirmed via DHCP (hostname DESKTOP-H8ALZBV, MAC bound to lease requests), NBNS (same hostname), ARP (MAC 00:1c:bf:03:54:82 bound to 10.8.15.133), and Kerberos CNameString (`plucero`, `DESKTOP-H8ALZBV$`).

### Malware family
**Attribution: behavioral, not signature-confirmed** (no alert export to corroborate). The delivery chain and beacon characteristics are consistent with a **DarkGate-style loader** — invoice-phishing ZIP with an oversized/padded JS downloader, followed by a `bitsadmin`-style fetch of a PE loader DLL, followed by HTTP beaconing to a bare-IP C2 using a spoofed legacy Internet Explorer 6 User-Agent and encrypted request/response bodies. No unique string/config was recovered to confirm the exact family name; treat "DarkGate" as the closest behavioral match, not a certainty.

**Observed chain:**
1. **t=74.7s** — Victim GETs `http://quote.checkfedexexp.com/managements?...` (FedEx-themed courier lure, Cloudflare-fronted). Server returns `Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="Invoice 876597035_003.zip"`.
2. Zip contains a single 6.99 MB JavaScript file, `Invoice-876597035-003-8331775-8334138.js`, padded with megabytes of scraped academic-text filler (MPI documentation, IPCC reports, etc.) to inflate size past AV/sandbox limits; only unobfuscated WSH call visible in cleartext is `WScript.Sleep(`.
3. **t=135.9s (≈61s later)** — Victim issues a `Microsoft BITS/7.8` HEAD then GET for `http://72.5.43.29/data/0f60a3e7baecf2748b1c8183ed37d1e4` — a 159,232-byte PE32+ DLL (x86-64) served mislabeled as `text/html`.
4. **t=196.9s onward (≈60s after the DLL lands)** — Victim begins repeated `GET /` and `POST /` to the same bare IP `72.5.43.29:80`, using `User-Agent: Mozilla / 5.0 (compatible; MSIE 6.0; Windows NT 5.1; SV1; .NET CLR 1.0.3705)`, with encrypted/binary POST bodies and a large opaque `Cookie` token carrying additional data. This beaconing continues at ~5-8s intervals through the end of the capture — classic C2 check-in behavior.

### Indicators of Compromise

| Type | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| c2_endpoint | 72.5.43.29:80 | Repeated GET/POST `/` beacons from victim starting frame ~11032 onward, spoofed MSIE6 UA, encrypted bodies, encrypted large Cookie token |
| url | `http://72.5.43.29/data/0f60a3e7baecf2748b1c8183ed37d1e4` | HTTP HEAD/GET via `Microsoft BITS/7.8` UA at t=135.9s; response is a 159,232-byte PE32+ DLL mislabeled `text/html` |
| domain | quote.checkfedexexp.com (104.21.55.70 / 172.67.170.159) | DNS resolution + HTTP host header serving the malicious ZIP |
| domain | business.checkfedexexp.com (172.67.170.159 / 23.220.251.208) | DNS resolution; referenced inside the downloader JS's padding/comment content alongside the lure |
| url | `http://quote.checkfedexexp.com/managements?16553a25e45250a41fd5&endeds=MIGpq&JStx=59bf050d37df88a9-ade43358-eaa1220b-0571422b-0f33e6aa150e86bafd0ed4&Ld=9d7502d88d752a27b1d00587309184b5a215` | GET at t=74.7s; response delivers `Invoice 876597035_003.zip` |
| file_name | Invoice 876597035_003.zip → contains Invoice-876597035-003-8331775-8334138.js | `Content-Disposition` header on the managements? response; extracted archive contents |
| file_hash | 798563fcf7600f7ef1a35996291a9dfb5f9902733404dd499e2e736ea1dc6fc5 (SHA256, the delivered ZIP) | Computed from HTTP-exported object for the managements? response |
| file_hash | dab98819d1d7677a60f5d06be210d45b74ae5fd8cf0c24ec1b3766e25ce6dc2c (SHA256, extracted .js downloader) | Computed after extracting the ZIP |
| file_hash | b7aec5f73d2a6bbd8cd920edb4760e2edadc98c3a45bf4fa994d47ca9cbd02f6 (SHA256, PE32+ DLL) | Computed from HTTP-exported object at `/data/0f60a3e7baecf2748b1c8183ed37d1e4` |

### Benign context (not indicators)
- `www.msftconnecttest.com`, `msedge.b.tlu.dl.delivery.mp.microsoft.com` (Windows/BITS OS telemetry and update delivery)
- `acroipm2.adobe.com`, `armmf.adobe.com` (Adobe telemetry)
- `oneclient.sfx.ms`, `r.msftstatic.com`, `sb.scorecardresearch.com`, `bzib.nelreports.net` (Microsoft 365/Firefox telemetry, analytics)
- SSDP M-SEARCH to 239.255.255.250, mDNS, LLMNR, DHCP, CLDAP/Kerberos/LDAP traffic to the domain controller 10.8.15.4 — normal Windows/AD chatter
- TeamViewer `din.aspx?...client=DynGate` signaling and `am_delta_patch_*.exe` (legitimate TeamViewer auto-update component present on the host; no evidence tying it to the intrusion)
- Two ambiguous artifacts (`foots.php`, `index.php?id=&subid=`) surfaced only as tshark's HTTP object-export filenames but did **not** correspond to any actual `http.request` in the capture and their "content" was empty or non-decodable binary — almost certainly a TLS/QUIC dissection artifact, not a real request. Excluded from IOCs since they cannot be grounded to real traffic.

**Summary:** DESKTOP-H8ALZBV (10.8.15.133, MAC 00:1c:bf:03:54:82), logged in as `plucero` on the LAFONTAINEBLEU domain, was compromised via a FedEx-themed invoice phishing page (`quote.checkfedexexp.com`) that delivered a padded/obfuscated JavaScript downloader inside a ZIP. That script pulled a PE32+ DLL payload from `72.5.43.29` via BITS, which then began persistent HTTP C2 beaconing to the same bare IP using a spoofed legacy Internet Explorer 6 User-Agent and encrypted traffic — behavior consistent with a DarkGate-style loader, though not signature-confirmed.
